---
title: "Return, Risk, and the Investor's Problem"
metadata:
  pagetitle: "Return, Risk, and the Investor's Problem"
  description-meta: "Return conventions, the excess-return basis, expected utility and risk aversion, mean-variance dominance, and where the risk-aversion parameter enters PortfolioAnalytics."
---



What does an investor want from a portfolio, and in which units should the
answer be measured? @markowitz1952 reduced the first question to two numbers
per portfolio, an expected return and a variance, and the reduction has held
up well enough that most of this book is built on it. The second question is
older and is usually skipped. @vonneumann1944 gave the criterion that ranks
risky prospects by their expected utility, and every mean-variance objective
is an approximation to that criterion whose quality depends on how a return
is defined, over which horizon, in which currency, and relative to which
riskless alternative. Those definitions are fixed here once, so that no later
chapter has to revisit them.

We first fix the return conventions: simple against log returns, arithmetic
against geometric means, annualization, and how a Sharpe ratio aggregates
over a horizon. We make excess returns the book's basis and say what nominal,
real and currency mean for it. We state the investor's problem as expected
utility, derive the mean-variance criterion and the certainty equivalent from
it, and say what the risk-aversion parameter $\gamma$ means in basis points.
We define mean-variance dominance and the northwest rule, show where $\gamma$
enters `PortfolioAnalytics` and what raising it does on the sixteen class
series, and close by defining strategic and tactical allocation for the rest
of the book. On that horizon axis this chapter is neither strategic nor
tactical: it is where the terms are defined, and the last part of
@sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-theory says which later chapters are
which.

The data are the sixteen risky class series of
@sec-02-notation-and-data-simulated-market, loaded as every chapter loads
them, in the symbols of @sec-02-notation-and-data-notation: $\boldsymbol{R}$
for the matrix of total returns, $r_f$ for the Treasury bill, $\boldsymbol{R}^e$
for the difference. The environment is the one
@sec-01-setting-up-implementation builds.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
R  <- as_xts_pm(sim_class_returns_monthly, date, class, return)   # sixteen risky classes
rf <- sim_riskfree_monthly$return                                  # the bill
Re <- R - rf                                                       # excess returns
stopifnot(ncol(R) == 16L, !anyNA(R),
          all(sim_riskfree_monthly$date == zoo::index(R)))         # same month ends
```
:::


## Returns, Horizons, and the Basis of Comparison {#sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-theory}

### Simple returns, log returns, and compounding

A simple return over one period is the change in value relative to the value
at the start, income included, and a log return is its logarithm:

$$
R_t = \frac{P_t + D_t}{P_{t-1}} - 1,
\qquad
r_t = \log\left(1 + R_t\right).
$$ {#eq-03-simple}

The two aggregate in opposite directions. Simple returns add across assets:
the return on a portfolio with weights $\boldsymbol{w}$ is
$\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{R}_t$, which is why every weight vector in this
book multiplies a matrix of simple returns. Log returns add across time. Over
$T$ periods,

$$
1 + R_{0,T} = \prod_{t=1}^{T}\left(1 + R_t\right) = \exp\left(\sum_{t=1}^{T} r_t\right),
$$ {#eq-03-compound}

so a multi-period simple return is a product and the matching log return is a
sum. The shipped data are simple monthly returns, and they stay simple
wherever a portfolio is formed. Log returns appear only where a horizon is
aggregated.

### Averages, annualization, and the variance drag

There are two averages of a return series and they answer different
questions. The arithmetic mean $\hat\mu = T^{-1}\sum_t R_t$ is the expected
one-period return and the quantity $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ that enters every
objective in this book, because variance is defined around it. The geometric
mean $g = \left(\prod_t (1 + R_t)\right)^{1/T} - 1$ is the constant return
that would have produced the same terminal wealth, and it is what an investor
who held the asset actually earned per period. To second order,

$$
\log(1 + g) \approx \mu - \frac{\sigma^2}{2},
$$ {#eq-03-drag}

where $\sigma^2$ is the variance of the simple return. The gap is the
**variance drag**, half the variance lost to compounding. It is small for a
government bond and not small for an equity market, and it lets a series have
the higher arithmetic mean and the lower geometric one, a case
@sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-application meets on this data.

Monthly moments are annualized by

$$
\mu_{\text{a}} = 12\,\mu_{\text{m}},
\qquad
\sigma_{\text{a}} = \sqrt{12}\,\sigma_{\text{m}},
\qquad
1 + g_{\text{a}} = \left(1 + g_{\text{m}}\right)^{12}.
$$ {#eq-03-annualize}

The first two follow from independence across months: the mean of a sum is
the sum of the means, and so is the variance, so the standard deviation grows
with the square root of the horizon. The third is compounding. Two mistakes
follow from mixing them. Multiplying a geometric monthly mean by twelve
understates the compounded annual return, and multiplying a monthly standard
deviation by $\sqrt{12}$ is wrong whenever monthly returns are
autocorrelated, because the variance of a sum then carries covariance terms
that independence set to zero.

### The Sharpe ratio and its horizon

The ratio of expected excess return to standard deviation was introduced by
@sharpe1966 as a measure of fund performance and restated by @sharpe1994 in
the form the industry uses:

$$
\text{SR} = \frac{\mu - r_f}{\sigma} = \frac{\mu^e}{\sigma^e}.
$$ {#eq-03-sharpe}

Under independence the numerator scales with $T$ and the denominator with
$\sqrt{T}$, so the ratio over $q$ periods is $\sqrt{q}$ times the one-period
ratio, and $\sqrt{12}$ turns a monthly Sharpe ratio into an annual one.
@lo2002 derived the general case. With autocorrelations $\rho_k$ at lags
$k = 1, \ldots, q - 1$,

$$
\text{SR}_q = \text{SR}_1 \cdot
\frac{q}{\sqrt{q + 2\sum_{k=1}^{q-1}(q - k)\,\rho_k}},
$$ {#eq-03-lo}

which reduces to $\sqrt{q}\,\text{SR}_1$ when every $\rho_k$ is zero.
Positive autocorrelation makes the naive $\sqrt{q}$ overstate the annual
ratio, negative autocorrelation makes it understate it, and
@sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-implementation measures the error on
this data.

### Excess returns as the basis

Every return this book optimizes over is measured in excess of the Treasury
bill,

$$
R^e_{it} = R_{it} - r_{f,t},
$$ {#eq-03-excess}

for four reasons, in increasing order of consequence.

First, the objects the theory talks about are defined relative to a riskless
rate. @tobin1958 showed that when a riskless asset exists, every investor
holds the same portfolio of risky assets and differs only in how much of it
is held against the riskless asset; the tangency portfolio at the center of
that result is the point where a ray from $r_f$ touches the frontier, and it
moves when $r_f$ moves. @sharpe1964 builds the market equilibrium on the same
portfolio. Neither exists without a riskless rate to measure from.

Second, `PortfolioAnalytics` has no argument for one. `optimize.portfolio()`
takes a return matrix and a specification, and its maximum-Sharpe objective
maximizes the ratio of mean to standard deviation over zero. Handing it excess
returns is the only way to make that ratio the Sharpe ratio of @eq-03-sharpe.

Third, when the weights may sum to less than one, the objective treats the
balance as earning exactly zero. With total returns that is false, because the
balance earns the bill. With excess returns it is true, because the balance
earns zero excess return. @sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-application
shows by how much the difference raises the invested fraction at the same
risk aversion.

Fourth, the bill moves. Under rebalancing the riskless rate is a different
number in every period, so a total-return objective compares each period's
assets against a different alternative, while the excess formulation
subtracts each period's own bill and is the only one consistent through time.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
rate <- sim_riskfree_monthly$rate_annual
c(first = rate[1], lowest = min(rate), highest = max(rate), last = rate[length(rate)])
#>   first  lowest highest    last 
#>  0.0384 -0.0001  0.0619  0.0430
```
:::


The bill paid 3.8% a year in
January of model year 1 and
-0.01% at its lowest, in
September of model year 24; an objective that
compares risky assets against zero in both periods is wrong in at least one.

The riskless rate is `sim_riskfree_monthly`, the three-month Treasury bill,
and not any of the five money-market series. Those are marked-to-market
quarter-year bonds, they carry duration, and they lose money in far more
months than the bill does; @sec-04-descriptive-analysis-implementation
measures the difference. A riskless asset has to be riskless over the holding
period, and only the bill is.

### Nominal and real

Every return above is nominal. A real return removes inflation $\pi$ through
the relation of @fisher1930,

$$
1 + i = (1 + r)(1 + \pi), \qquad r \approx i - \pi,
$$ {#eq-03-fisher}

with $i$ the nominal and $r$ the real rate. The modeled market carries no
inflation series, so this book works in nominal dollars throughout, and the
bill is riskless in nominal terms only. An investor whose liabilities are
real, a pension fund or an endowment spending a fixed share of purchasing
power, would measure every return in excess of realized inflation, would find
the bill risky over any horizon longer than its maturity, and would treat an
inflation-indexed bond as the riskless asset. @campbell2002 develop that
investor's problem in full, and @campbell2001 show that for a long-horizon
investor the indexed bond, not the bill, is the safe asset. Nothing in the
machinery of later chapters changes for such an investor; only the series
handed to it does.

### Currency

Every series in the modeled market is a dollar return, unhedged. A foreign
asset's dollar return compounds its local return with the return $f_t$ on its
currency, quoted as dollars per unit of local currency so that a positive
$f_t$ means the local currency appreciated:

$$
1 + R^{\$}_t = \left(1 + R^{\text{loc}}_t\right)\left(1 + f_t\right),
\qquad
R^{\text{hedged}}_t = R^{\$}_t - f_t \approx R^{\text{loc}}_t .
$$ {#eq-03-currency}

Hedging in this book is therefore a subtraction: the matching `fx_return`
from `sim_fx_monthly` is removed from the unhedged series, to first order. A
forward hedge also earns the interest differential between the two
currencies, which the data do not carry, so the convention is the spot
return alone, and @sec-15-hierarchical-allocation-implementation and
@sec-22-fixed-income-sleeve-theory keep it. @perold1988 argued that hedging
removes volatility at no expected cost, a free lunch; @black1989 derived a
single universal hedge ratio for every investor; @campbell2010 found that the
answer differs between bonds, which should be fully hedged, and equities,
whose currencies covary with the local market in ways that sometimes hedge
them for free. @sec-04-descriptive-analysis-application decomposes the
variance of a foreign series into its local and currency parts, and
@sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-implementation shows what the
subtraction does to a foreign government bond.

### The investor's objective

Write $W_0$ for initial wealth, $\boldsymbol{w}$ for the weights on the risky
assets, and $1 - \boldsymbol{\iota}'\boldsymbol{w}$ for the balance in the
bill. The investor of @vonneumann1944 chooses the weights that maximize the
expected utility of terminal wealth,

$$
\max_{\boldsymbol{w}} \; \mathbb{E}\!\left[U(W_1)\right],
\qquad
W_1 = W_0\left(1 + r_f + \boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{R}^e\right),
$$ {#eq-03-expected-utility}

for a utility function $U$ that is increasing and concave. Concavity is risk
aversion, and @pratt1964 and @arrow1965 measured it: the coefficient of
absolute risk aversion is $A(W) = -U''(W)/U'(W)$, the coefficient of relative
risk aversion is $\gamma(W) = W A(W)$, and an investor with relative risk
aversion $\gamma$ facing a return with variance $\sigma^2$ demands a premium,
as a fraction of wealth, of approximately

$$
\text{premium} \approx \tfrac{1}{2}\,\gamma\,\sigma^2 .
$$ {#eq-03-arrow-pratt}

A second-order expansion of @eq-03-expected-utility around expected terminal
wealth turns it into a function of two moments. Dropping the terms that do
not depend on $\boldsymbol{w}$, the investor maximizes

$$
U(\boldsymbol{w}) = \mu_{\boldsymbol{w}} - \frac{\gamma}{2}\,\sigma^2_{\boldsymbol{w}}
= \boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\mu} - \frac{\gamma}{2}\,\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w},
$$ {#eq-03-quadratic-utility}

with $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ the mean vector and
covariance matrix of the excess returns. This is the mean-variance criterion
of @markowitz1952, and @markowitz1959 gave the two conditions under which the
expansion is exact: $U$ is itself quadratic, or returns are normal so that
every higher moment is a function of the first two. Neither holds for the
series of this book, and the question is what that costs. @levy1979 compared
the expected utility of the mean-variance optimum with that of the true
optimum across utility functions and historical returns and found the two
almost perfectly correlated; @markowitz2014 revisited the evidence with thirty
more years of data and reached the same conclusion. The approximation fails
where returns are far from normal, and @sec-11-higher-moments-theory takes
up that case by adding skewness and kurtosis to @eq-03-quadratic-utility
rather than abandoning it.

Two readings of @eq-03-quadratic-utility are worth having. First,
$U(\boldsymbol{w})$ is a certainty equivalent: the riskless excess return the
investor would accept in place of the portfolio, the expected return less the
premium of @eq-03-arrow-pratt applied to the portfolio's own variance.
Second, $\gamma$ is a price. Along an indifference curve $U(\boldsymbol{w})$
is constant, so an increase in expected return of $\Delta\mu$ buys an
increase in variance of

$$
\sigma_1^2 - \sigma_0^2 = \frac{2\,\Delta\mu}{\gamma},
$$ {#eq-03-tradeoff}

and the price has units. With $\Delta\mu$ one percentage point and
$\sigma_0 = 0$, an investor with $\gamma = 2$ accepts a volatility of
$\sqrt{0.02 / 2} = 10.0%$ for one
point of expected return; one with $\gamma = 10$ accepts
$\sqrt{0.02 / 10} = 4.5%$. Read the
other way, ten percent of volatility costs an investor with $\gamma = 4$ a
certainty equivalent of $\tfrac{4}{2} \times 0.10^2 =
200$ basis points a year.


::: {#tbl-03-gamma .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='What the risk-aversion parameter means in units an investor recognizes. Each row is computed from @eq-03-tradeoff with one percentage point of expected return on one side, from cash and from a portfolio with ten percent volatility, and from @eq-03-quadratic-utility for the certainty-equivalent cost of ten percent volatility.'}
::: {.cell-output-display}


| $\gamma$| volatility accepted for +1 pp, from cash| extra volatility accepted for +1 pp, from 10%| certainty-equivalent cost of 10% volatility|
|--------:|----------------------------------------:|---------------------------------------------:|-------------------------------------------:|
|        1|                                    14.1%|                                       +7.3 pp|                                       50 bp|
|        2|                                    10.0%|                                       +4.1 pp|                                      100 bp|
|        3|                                     8.2%|                                       +2.9 pp|                                      150 bp|
|        5|                                     6.3%|                                       +1.8 pp|                                      250 bp|
|        8|                                     5.0%|                                       +1.2 pp|                                      400 bp|
|       10|                                     4.5%|                                       +1.0 pp|                                      500 bp|
|       15|                                     3.7%|                                       +0.6 pp|                                      750 bp|
|       20|                                     3.2%|                                       +0.5 pp|                                     1000 bp|


:::
:::


@tbl-03-gamma is the table to keep in mind whenever a chapter reports a
$\gamma$. The customary range in the literature runs from about two to about
ten, and the data give one more anchor: an investor who holds the US equity
market and nothing else, and is at an optimum, has $\gamma = \mu^e / \sigma^2$
by the first-order condition of @eq-03-quadratic-utility with one asset.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
mu_us <- mean(Re[, "US_equity"]) * 12
sd_us <- stats::sd(Re[, "US_equity"]) * sqrt(12)
c(excess_return = mu_us, volatility = sd_us, implied_gamma = mu_us / sd_us^2)
#> excess_return    volatility implied_gamma 
#>        0.1130        0.1562        4.6332
```
:::


On this sample that investor has $\gamma = 0.113 /
0.156^2 = 4.6$.

The alternative to quadratic utility that the rest of the literature uses is
constant relative risk aversion, $U(W) = W^{1-\gamma}/(1-\gamma)$, under
which the premium of @eq-03-arrow-pratt is the same fraction of wealth at
every level of wealth. When returns are lognormal, maximizing expected power
utility is equivalent to maximizing $\mu - \tfrac{\gamma}{2}\sigma^2$ in log
returns with the same $\gamma$, so the two objectives agree exactly on that
distribution and approximately on any distribution close to it. The
disagreements are in the tails, and @sec-11-higher-moments-theory measures
them on the credit series where they matter.

### The horizon of the problem

@eq-03-expected-utility is a one-period problem, and a reader may object that
the investor lives for many. @samuelson1969 in discrete time and @merton1969
in continuous time solved the multi-period problem for a power-utility
investor and found that when returns are independent across periods and the
investment opportunities do not change, the optimal weights are the same in
every period and at every horizon: the long-lived investor behaves myopically,
and the one-period rule is exact. When opportunities do change, because the
riskless rate or the expected returns move, the long-horizon investor holds
additional positions that hedge those changes, which is the case
@campbell2002 treat and the reason their safe asset is the indexed bond. This
book solves the one-period problem throughout and re-solves it at each
rebalancing date, which is the myopic policy; the chapters on the horizon
axis, defined below, are about how the inputs to that policy are formed
rather than about intertemporal hedging.

### Dominance, efficiency, and the northwest rule

Two moments per portfolio make comparison a matter of geometry. In the plane
with volatility on the horizontal axis and expected return on the vertical,
portfolio $A$ **dominates** portfolio $B$ if it offers at least as much return
for at most as much risk, with strictly more of one or strictly less of the
other:

$$
A \succ B
\iff
\mu_A \ge \mu_B \;\text{ and }\; \sigma_A \le \sigma_B,
\;\text{ with at least one inequality strict.}
$$ {#eq-03-dominance}

The relation has a direction. A dominating portfolio lies above, to the left,
or both: **a better allocation always lies to the northwest**. A portfolio or
asset that no feasible alternative dominates is **efficient**, and the set of
efficient portfolios is the efficient frontier that
@sec-09-mean-variance-theory derives. @eq-03-dominance is weaker than
@eq-03-quadratic-utility, because it ranks only pairs one of which is
northwest of the other and says nothing about a pair where one has more
return and more risk; the utility function settles those by choosing a point
on the frontier. It is also stronger in one respect: a dominated portfolio is
rejected by every investor with any $\gamma > 0$, so the vocabulary applies
before a risk aversion is chosen, and every chapter from here on uses
*dominated* and *efficient* in this sense.

### Strategic and tactical allocation

Two distinct cuts run through the book and are easily confused. The first is
granularity: allocate across asset classes, then select within a class, which
is the order of the parts. The second is horizon, and it needs two terms that
are defined here once.

**Strategic allocation** is the long-run policy: the portfolio an investor
would hold given unconditional beliefs about the assets, with $\boldsymbol{\mu}$
and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ estimated over the whole available history and no
attempt to time anything. **Tactical allocation** is a deviation from that
policy using conditioning information available at the time: a signal, a
regime, a view. The two are orthogonal to granularity, because a tactical
tilt can be taken across classes and a permanent tilt inside a sleeve is
strategic. @brinson1986 and @brinson1991 measured how much of the variation
in a set of pension funds' returns the policy alone explained and found most
of it; @ibbotson2000 clarified what that number does and does not mean, in
particular that it says nothing about the level of return the policy earns.
@sharpe1987 gave the framework in which the two are stages of one decision,
the policy set from capital-market assumptions and the tactical position from
the same assumptions updated with current information, and @ang2014 organizes
an entire treatment of asset management around the strategic question of
which bad times an investor can bear. The strategic policy is itself an
estimate from a finite history, and @demiguel2009 measured what that costs
out of sample.

The chapters of this book sort as follows. Chapters 9 to 14 and chapter 15
are strategic: they solve @eq-03-quadratic-utility and its relatives from
full-sample moments, and @sec-09-mean-variance-theory opens by saying so.
Chapters 16 to 19 are tactical: they condition the inputs on information
available at the time, beginning with @sec-16-signals-and-forecasts-theory.
Chapters 23 to 25 are about implementation and evaluation of either, and
@sec-25-backtesting-application is where the strategic policies of Part IV
are finally run as they would have been run. Each chapter says which it is
doing in its opening paragraph.

One rule follows from the objective and applies on either axis. The measure a
portfolio is judged by must be the measure it was chosen by. A portfolio that
minimizes expected shortfall and is then reported on its Sharpe ratio has
been misreported: it was never asked to maximize that ratio, and its
shortfall, the quantity it was built for, has gone unmentioned. @artzner1999
and @acerbi2002 give the properties a risk measure should have;
@sec-10-risk-measures-theory chooses among them, and
@sec-25-backtesting-application reports every strategy on every measure so
that the reader can see which portfolio won on which criterion.

## Implementation {#sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-implementation}

### Return conventions in `PerformanceAnalytics`

`PerformanceAnalytics` implements every convention above, and the point of
showing them is to see which convention each function defaults to. The class
tables ship a total-return index, so a price series can be rebuilt and
@eq-03-simple checked against the shipped return.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
us <- dplyr::filter(sim_class_returns_monthly, class == "US_equity")
P  <- xts::xts(us$index, order.by = us$date)

simple <- Return.calculate(P, method = "discrete")
logret <- Return.calculate(P, method = "log")
stopifnot(all.equal(as.numeric(simple[-1]), as.numeric(R[-1, "US_equity"])))
head(merge(simple, logret, shipped = R[, "US_equity"]), 3)
#>              simple   logret US_equity
#> 2101-01-31       NA       NA  0.025013
#> 2101-02-28 0.022790 0.022534  0.022790
#> 2101-03-31 0.005306 0.005292  0.005306
```
:::


The first observation is `NA`, because a return needs two prices. The log
return is smaller than the simple one when the simple return is positive and
larger in absolute value when it is negative, which is @eq-03-simple.

`Return.annualized()` with `scale = 1` returns the per-period geometric mean,
because it evaluates $\left(\prod (1 + R_t)\right)^{\text{scale}/T} - 1$, so
the two averages and the drag between them come from one series.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
x    <- R[, "US_equity"]
mu_m <- mean(x)                                          # arithmetic, monthly
g_m  <- as.numeric(Return.annualized(x, scale = 1))      # geometric, monthly
s2_m <- stats::var(as.numeric(x))
c(arithmetic = mu_m, geometric = g_m, gap = mu_m - g_m, half_variance = s2_m / 2)
#>    arithmetic     geometric           gap half_variance 
#>      0.011284      0.010262      0.001022      0.001019
```
:::


::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Worked: the drag of @eq-03-drag on `US_equity`

With the sample numbers substituted, the drag is

$$
\mu - g
= 0.011284 - 0.010262
= 0.001022,
\qquad
\frac{\sigma^2}{2} = \frac{0.002038}{2} = 0.001019,
$$

and the two agree to 3.0e-06, which
is the third-order term @eq-03-drag drops. The drag is
10.2 basis points a month, or
1.23 percentage points a year on a
series with 15.6% annualized
volatility.
:::

Annualizing the same series under the three conventions of @eq-03-annualize
gives three different numbers, and the package's default is the compounded
one.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
c(arithmetic_x12    = as.numeric(Return.annualized(x, scale = 12, geometric = FALSE)),
  compounded        = as.numeric(Return.annualized(x, scale = 12)),          # the default
  cumulative        = as.numeric(Return.cumulative(x)),
  volatility_sqrt12 = as.numeric(StdDev.annualized(x, scale = 12)))
#>    arithmetic_x12        compounded        cumulative volatility_sqrt12 
#>            0.1354            0.1303           43.6152            0.1564
```
:::


A dollar in `US_equity` at the start of the sample became
44.6 dollars by its end,
which is $\left(1 + 0.1303\right)^{31}$
to rounding and not $1 + 31 \times 0.1354$. The
arithmetic figure is the right input to @eq-03-quadratic-utility and the
wrong answer to the question of what the asset paid.

### The Sharpe ratio, in two conventions

`Return.excess()` implements @eq-03-excess and reproduces the subtraction of
the data block exactly, so the two routes to `Re` cannot drift apart.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
bill  <- xts::xts(rf, order.by = zoo::index(R)); colnames(bill) <- "bill"
Re_pa <- Return.excess(R, Rf = bill)
stopifnot(all.equal(zoo::coredata(Re_pa), zoo::coredata(Re), check.attributes = FALSE))
```
:::


`table.AnnualizedReturns()` reports the compounded return, the annualized
volatility and a Sharpe ratio per series; `SharpeRatio.annualized()` reports
the last of these on its own. On the same series they disagree.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
three <- c("US_equity", "US_credit", "US_government")
table.AnnualizedReturns(R[, three], scale = 12, Rf = bill)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   US_equity US_credit US_government
#>       <dbl>     <dbl>         <dbl>
#> 1     0.130    0.063         0.0454
#> 2     0.156    0.0725        0.0478
#> 3     0.676    0.545         0.469
SharpeRatio.annualized(R[, three], Rf = bill, scale = 12)
#>                                           US_equity US_credit US_government
#> Annualized Sharpe Ratio (Rf=2.2%, p=95%):    0.7236    0.5726        0.4882
```
:::


::: {.callout-note}
## Two functions, two defaults for the same ratio

`table.AnnualizedReturns()` defaults to `geometric = TRUE` and divides the
compounded excess return by the annualized volatility.
`SharpeRatio.annualized()` defaults to `geometric = FALSE` and divides twelve
times the arithmetic monthly excess return by the same volatility, which is
$\sqrt{12}$ times the monthly ratio of @eq-03-sharpe. The gap is the drag of
@eq-03-drag divided by the volatility, so it grows with the volatility of the
series, and it can reorder a ranking. Either convention is defensible; mixing
them across a table is not. When this book reports the Sharpe ratio of a
series it uses the compounded convention, as
@sec-04-descriptive-analysis-implementation does; when it optimizes, the
objective contains the arithmetic mean, because that is what
@eq-03-quadratic-utility is a function of.
:::

The reordering is visible on the sixteen series, and both rankings come from
one function with the convention as an argument.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
sr_compounded <- SharpeRatio.annualized(R, Rf = bill, scale = 12, geometric = TRUE)[1, colnames(R)]
sr_arithmetic <- SharpeRatio.annualized(R, Rf = bill, scale = 12, geometric = FALSE)[1, colnames(R)]
rank_of <- function(s, a) as.integer(rank(-s)[[a]])

sr_rank <- tibble::tibble(
  asset           = colnames(R),
  volatility      = unname(StdDev.annualized(R, scale = 12)[1, asset]),
  rank_arithmetic = as.integer(rank(-sr_arithmetic[asset])),
  rank_compounded = as.integer(rank(-sr_compounded[asset]))
)
moved <- dplyr::filter(sr_rank, rank_arithmetic != rank_compounded)

# Pairs that trade places under compounding: one series falls, one rises.
swaps <- dplyr::inner_join(
  dplyr::filter(moved, rank_compounded > rank_arithmetic),
  dplyr::filter(moved, rank_compounded < rank_arithmetic),
  by = c(rank_arithmetic = "rank_compounded", rank_compounded = "rank_arithmetic"),
  suffix = c("_falls", "_rises"))
stopifnot(2L * nrow(swaps) == nrow(moved), nrow(swaps) > 0L,       # every move is a swap
          all(swaps$volatility_falls > swaps$volatility_rises),
          names(which.max(sr_compounded)) == names(which.max(sr_arithmetic)),
          rank_of(sr_compounded, "US_credit") == rank_of(sr_arithmetic, "US_credit"))
dplyr::select(swaps, asset_falls, asset_rises, rank_arithmetic, rank_compounded)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   asset_falls      asset_rises   rank_arithmetic rank_compounded
#>   <chr>            <chr>                   <int>           <int>
#> 1 CH_equity        US_government               5               6
#> 2 GLOBAL_commodity CH_government              11              12
#> 3 JP_equity        EU_credit                   9              10
#> 4 UK_credit        CH_credit                   7               8
```
:::


The two conventions agree on the top of the ranking:
`US_equity` is first under
both, and `US_credit` ranks 3 of sixteen
under both. Elsewhere 8 series change rank, always two at a
time trading places: under compounding
`CH_equity` falls behind `US_government`, `GLOBAL_commodity` falls behind `CH_government`, `JP_equity` falls behind `EU_credit`, `UK_credit` falls behind `CH_credit`.
In each of the 4 pairs the series that falls is the more
volatile one, whose drag is larger, and the `stopifnot()` asserts it.

### Aggregation over horizons

@eq-03-lo says when $\sqrt{12}$ is the right factor. The direct test is to
compound the monthly series to quarters and years and compute the ratio at
each horizon.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
sr <- function(v) mean(v) / stats::sd(v)
by_horizon <- function(series) {
  z <- Re[, series]
  q <- xts::apply.quarterly(z, function(v) prod(1 + v) - 1)
  y <- xts::apply.yearly(z,    function(v) prod(1 + v) - 1)
  c(monthly_x_sqrt12 = sr(z) * sqrt(12), quarterly_x_2 = sr(q) * 2, annual = sr(y))
}
horizons  <- rbind(US_equity = by_horizon("US_equity"),
                   US_government = by_horizon("US_government"))
shortfall <- 1 - horizons[, "annual"] / horizons[, "monthly_x_sqrt12"]
rho1      <- apply(Re, 2, function(v) stats::acf(as.numeric(v), lag.max = 1, plot = FALSE)$acf[2])
stopifnot(shortfall[["US_government"]] > shortfall[["US_equity"]], shortfall[["US_equity"]] > 0,
          rho1[["US_government"]] > 0.1, abs(rho1[["US_equity"]]) < 0.05)
round(cbind(horizons, shortfall, rho1 = rho1[rownames(horizons)]), 3)
#>               monthly_x_sqrt12 quarterly_x_2 annual shortfall   rho1
#> US_equity                0.724         0.663  0.652     0.098 -0.004
#> US_government            0.488         0.417  0.379     0.224  0.147
```
:::


For `US_government` the annual ratio is
22% below the
$\sqrt{12}$ figure, because its monthly returns have a first-order
autocorrelation of 0.147: the variance
of a twelve-month sum exceeds twelve monthly variances, and the annual ratio
falls short of $\sqrt{12}$ times the monthly one. For `US_equity` the annual
ratio is 10% below it,
and a first-order autocorrelation of
-0.004 does not explain that. The
correction of @eq-03-lo, applied to every series, says how far the naive
factor is off on account of autocorrelation at every lag.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
lo_factor <- function(v, q = 12) {
  rho <- stats::acf(as.numeric(v), lag.max = q - 1, plot = FALSE)$acf[-1]
  q / sqrt(q + 2 * sum((q - seq_len(q - 1)) * rho))
}
lo_ratio  <- apply(Re, 2, lo_factor) / sqrt(12)   # 1 means sqrt(12) was right
lo_sorted <- sort(lo_ratio)
round(lo_sorted, 3)
#>    US_government        EU_credit        JP_credit        US_credit 
#>            0.867            0.870            0.875            0.876 
#>    EU_government    JP_government        UK_credit        JP_equity 
#>            0.894            0.913            0.936            0.937 
#> GLOBAL_commodity        US_equity        CH_credit        UK_equity 
#>            0.947            0.970            1.020            1.022 
#>        EU_equity        CH_equity    UK_government    CH_government 
#>            1.033            1.033            1.047            1.068

# The largest overstatements lead with bond and credit series.
n_lead <- which(!grepl("_(government|credit)$", names(lo_sorted)))[1] - 1L
stopifnot(n_lead >= 5L, all(lo_sorted[seq_len(n_lead)] < 1),
          all(rho1[names(lo_sorted)[seq_len(n_lead)]] > 0),
          all(1 - lo_ratio[names(shortfall)] < shortfall))
```
:::


The naive factor overstates the annual Sharpe ratio of
10 of the sixteen series,
`US_government` most, by
15%, and understates that of
the other 6,
`CH_government` most, by
6%; the median correction
across the sixteen is 7%.
The 7 largest overstatements are all on government and credit
series, whose monthly returns are positively autocorrelated. The correction
puts the annual ratio of `US_government`
13% below the
$\sqrt{12}$ figure, where the direct calculation had it
22% below, and that of
`US_equity` 3% below
against 10%. The rest is
not autocorrelation: the direct figure rests on 31 annual
observations and is itself imprecise. $\sqrt{12}$ is the convention this book
uses, with that caveat attached.

### The bill is not a seventeenth asset

A reader who has just been told that the riskless rate is essential will be
tempted to add it to the return matrix as another column. With the actual bill
as a seventeenth column, a minimum-variance optimizer buys almost nothing
else; with a constant riskless rate, the covariance matrix loses rank and
cannot be inverted, which is why @tobin1958 treats the riskless asset
separately in the algebra rather than as one more row of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
gmv_of <- function(X) {
  spec <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(X)) |>
    add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
    add.constraint(type = "long_only") |>
    add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var")
  w <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(X, spec, optimize_method = "ROI"))
  w[colnames(X)]
}
R_bill  <- merge(R, bill)
R_const <- merge(R, constant = xts::xts(rep(mean(rf), nrow(R)), order.by = zoo::index(R)))

w_bill <- gmv_of(R_bill)
round(w_bill[w_bill > 0.001], 4)
#> CH_credit JP_equity      bill 
#>    0.0034    0.0021    0.9941
c(rank_with_bill = qr(stats::cov(R_bill))$rank, rank_with_constant = qr(stats::cov(R_const))$rank)
#>     rank_with_bill rank_with_constant 
#>                 17                 16
```
:::


The optimizer puts 99.4% into the
bill, and the constant column leaves a 17-by-17
covariance matrix of rank 16. The riskless
asset enters through the excess-return basis and the budget constraint, not
through the covariance matrix.

### Hedging a foreign government bond

@eq-03-currency is one subtraction per series, and the four foreign
government bonds are where it matters most, because a government bond has
little local volatility to begin with.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
fx <- sim_fx_monthly
hedge_stats <- function(series, region) {
  f <- fx$fx_return[fx$region == region]
  stopifnot(all(fx$date[fx$region == region] == zoo::index(R)))   # same months
  u <- as.numeric(R[, series])
  c(unhedged = stats::sd(u) * sqrt(12), hedged = stats::sd(u - f) * sqrt(12))
}
govs <- tibble::tibble(region = c("EU", "UK", "CH", "JP"),
                       series = paste0(region, "_government"))
hedged_govs <- govs |>
  dplyr::mutate(stats = purrr::map2(series, region, hedge_stats),
                unhedged = purrr::map_dbl(stats, "unhedged"),
                hedged   = purrr::map_dbl(stats, "hedged"),
                removed  = 1 - hedged / unhedged) |>
  dplyr::select(series, unhedged, hedged, removed)
hedged_govs
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   series        unhedged hedged removed
#>   <chr>            <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 EU_government   0.0981 0.0390   0.603
#> 2 UK_government   0.0951 0.0475   0.500
#> 3 CH_government   0.109  0.0335   0.693
#> 4 JP_government   0.107  0.0312   0.709
```
:::


Hedging removes between
50% and
71% of a foreign government
bond's volatility. `JP_government` goes from
10.7%
to
3.1%:
71%
of what a dollar investor experiences as bond volatility in that series is
exchange rate. Whether the same holds for an equity market is a
different question with a different answer, and
@sec-04-descriptive-analysis-application gives it.

### Where risk aversion enters the package

`PortfolioAnalytics` states @eq-03-quadratic-utility as two objectives on one
specification: a return objective named `mean` and a risk objective named
`var` carrying a `risk_aversion` argument. `quadratic_utility_objective()`
builds the same pair in one call, to be assigned to the specification's
`objectives` slot. Before either is used, one thing about the argument has to
be known.

::: {.callout-warning}
## `risk_aversion` is $\gamma/2$, not $\gamma$

The package builds $\boldsymbol{Q} = 2\lambda\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ from
`risk_aversion = `$\lambda$ and hands it to `ROI`, whose quadratic program is
stated as $\tfrac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{x}'\boldsymbol{Q}\boldsymbol{x}$. The two
factors of two do not cancel: the coefficient on
$\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}$ in the solved problem is
$\lambda$, where @eq-03-quadratic-utility puts $\gamma/2$. To solve the
problem a textbook writes with $\gamma$, pass `risk_aversion = `$\gamma/2$.
The behavior is undocumented upstream, the derivation is in
@sec-91-proofs-quadratic-utility, and the check below verifies it numerically
on this data. Every $\gamma$ in this book is the textbook one, and every call
halves it.
:::


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
base_spec <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
  add.constraint(type = "long_only")

qu_spec <- function(spec, gamma) {
  spec |>
    add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
    add.objective(type = "risk",   name = "var", risk_aversion = gamma / 2)
}

pa_weights <- function(spec, gamma) {
  w <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(Re, qu_spec(spec, gamma), optimize_method = "ROI"))
  w[colnames(Re)]
}

# The same objective through the package's own constructor.
spec_qu <- base_spec
spec_qu$objectives <- quadratic_utility_objective(risk_aversion = 10 / 2)
w_ctor <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(Re, spec_qu, optimize_method = "ROI"))[colnames(Re)]
stopifnot(all.equal(pa_weights(base_spec, gamma = 10), w_ctor))
round(w_ctor[w_ctor > 0.005], 4)
#>     EU_equity     US_credit     US_equity US_government 
#>        0.1499        0.0611        0.2838        0.5038
```
:::


The check is a second solver that takes $\gamma$ literally. `quadprog`
minimizes $\tfrac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{x}'\boldsymbol{D}\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{d}'\boldsymbol{x}$,
so $\boldsymbol{D} = \gamma\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ and $\boldsymbol{d} = \boldsymbol{\mu}$
is exactly the negative of @eq-03-quadratic-utility. The weights may sum to
anything between zero and one, because a budget that binds would hide the
scale on which the two conventions differ.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
mu <- colMeans(Re)
S  <- stats::cov(Re)

relaxed_spec <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "weight_sum", min_sum = 0, max_sum = 1) |>   # 0 <= sum(w) <= 1
  add.constraint(type = "long_only")

qp_weights <- function(gamma) {
  n <- ncol(Re)
  w <- quadprog::solve.QP(Dmat = gamma * S, dvec = mu,
                          Amat = cbind(-rep(1, n), diag(n)),        # -sum(w) >= -1, w >= 0
                          bvec = c(-1, rep(0, n)))$solution
  setNames(w, colnames(Re))
}

gamma0 <- 10
w_pa   <- pa_weights(relaxed_spec, gamma0)                  # passes risk_aversion = 5
c(gap_if_argument_is_half_gamma = max(abs(w_pa - qp_weights(gamma0))),
  gap_if_argument_is_gamma      = max(abs(w_pa - qp_weights(gamma0 / 2))))
#> gap_if_argument_is_half_gamma      gap_if_argument_is_gamma 
#>          0.000000000000000451          0.400563221028796157
```
:::


The package's answer at `risk_aversion = 5` matches the textbook problem at
$\gamma = 10$ to machine precision and misses the one at $\gamma = 5$ by
0.40 in the largest
weight. The claim of the callout is measured rather than asserted.

## What the Objective Does on Sixteen Assets {#sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-application}

### The northwest rule applied

The application opens with the picture. Each series is one point in the plane
of @eq-03-dominance, with the arithmetic excess mean on the vertical axis
because that is what $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ is, and every coordinate is assembled
into one data frame before anything is drawn, so that a volatility can never
be paired with another asset's return.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
mom <- tibble::tibble(
  asset = colnames(Re),
  mu    = as.numeric(colMeans(Re)) * 12,                # arithmetic excess, annualized
  sigma = as.numeric(apply(Re, 2, stats::sd)) * sqrt(12)
)
n_dominating <- function(i) sum(mom$mu >= mom$mu[i] & mom$sigma <= mom$sigma[i]) - 1L
mom$dominated_by <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(mom)), n_dominating, integer(1))
mom$kind         <- ifelse(mom$dominated_by > 0L, "dominated", "efficient")
mom <- dplyr::arrange(mom, dplyr::desc(mu))
stopifnot(setequal(mom$asset, colnames(Re)))
```

### Raising $\gamma$ under full investment

With the weights forced to sum to one, raising $\gamma$ walks the solution
along the efficient frontier toward its left end and stops there. It does not
reach cash, because there is no cash to reach: the whole portfolio must be in
the sixteen risky series, and the least risky thing they can form is the
minimum-variance portfolio of @sec-09-mean-variance-theory.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
p_vol <- function(w) sqrt(as.numeric(t(w) %*% S %*% w)) * sqrt(12)
p_ret <- function(w) sum(mu * w) * 12

w_gmv <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(
  Re, base_spec |> add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var"),
  optimize_method = "ROI"))[colnames(Re)]

gammas <- c(1, 2, 4, 10, 20, 50, 100, 1000, 10000)
sweep_full <- purrr::map_dfr(gammas, function(g) {
  w <- pa_weights(base_spec, g)
  tibble::tibble(gamma = g, rule = "fully invested", invested = sum(w),
                 vol = p_vol(w), ret = p_ret(w), largest = max(w),
                 to_gmv = sum(abs(w - w_gmv)) / 2)
})
```

### Relaxing full investment

Let the weights sum to anything between zero and one, so that the balance
sits in the bill at zero excess return. Without the budget constraint the
first-order condition of @eq-03-quadratic-utility is
$\boldsymbol{\mu} = \gamma\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}$, so that

$$
\boldsymbol{w}^\ast(\gamma) = \frac{1}{\gamma}\,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\iota}'\boldsymbol{w}^\ast(\gamma) = \frac{\boldsymbol{\iota}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}}{\gamma}:
$$ {#eq-03-separation}

the composition of the risky holdings does not depend on $\gamma$, and the
invested fraction is proportional to $1/\gamma$. That is @tobin1958's
separation with the algebra written out, and it survives the long-only
constraint, because scaling a feasible long-only vector keeps it feasible.
The cap at one adds only a range of small $\gamma$ over which the investor
would borrow and is not allowed to.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
sweep_relaxed <- purrr::map_dfr(c(gammas, 1e5), function(g) {
  w <- pa_weights(relaxed_spec, g)
  tibble::tibble(gamma = g, rule = "budget relaxed", invested = sum(w),
                 vol = p_vol(w), ret = p_ret(w), largest = max(w), to_gmv = NA_real_)
})

# Composition is invariant once the cap stops binding: same risky portfolio, rescaled.
comp <- lapply(c(50, 1000), function(g) { w <- pa_weights(relaxed_spec, g); w / sum(w) })
stopifnot(all.equal(comp[[1]], comp[[2]], tolerance = 1e-6))

k <- with(dplyr::filter(sweep_relaxed, invested < 0.999), invested * gamma)
stopifnot(diff(range(k)) < 1e-6)                       # invested * gamma is a constant
sweep_relaxed |>
  dplyr::transmute(gamma, invested_x_gamma = round(invested * gamma, 2),   # before rounding
                   invested = round(invested, 4), vol = round(vol, 5)) |>
  as.data.frame()
#> # A tibble: 10 × 4
#>     gamma invested_x_gamma invested     vol
#>     <dbl>            <dbl>    <dbl>   <dbl>
#>  1      1              1     1      0.200  
#>  2      2              2     1      0.167  
#>  3      4              4     1      0.145  
#>  4     10             10     1      0.0707 
#>  5     20             19.4   0.967  0.0495 
#>  6     50             19.4   0.387  0.0198 
#>  7    100             19.4   0.194  0.00991
#>  8   1000             19.4   0.0193 0.00099
#>  9  10000             19.4   0.0019 0.0001 
#> 10 100000             19.4   0.0002 0.00001
```
:::


The cap binds up to $\gamma$ of about 19; beyond it
the invested fraction is exactly 19.35$/\gamma$:
19.3% at $\gamma = 100$ and
0.019% at $\gamma = 100{,}000$. The risky
part of the portfolio is the same at every one of those levels, which the
`stopifnot()` asserts rather than assumes, and it is the long-only portfolio
with the highest Sharpe ratio, the one @sec-09-mean-variance-implementation
reads off the frontier. The very risk-averse investor who may hold the bill
holds almost nothing else; the one who may not holds the minimum-variance
portfolio. Same $\gamma$, different budget rule, different answer, and
@fig-03-gamma shows both.

### The basis, once more, in the invested fraction

The third argument for excess returns in
@sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-theory can now be measured. Hand the
same relaxed problem total returns instead of excess returns and the
optimizer believes the alternative to the risky series earns zero rather than
the bill.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
invested_on <- function(X, gamma) {
  spec <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(X)) |>
    add.constraint(type = "weight_sum", min_sum = 0, max_sum = 1) |>
    add.constraint(type = "long_only")
  sum(extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(X, qu_spec(spec, gamma), optimize_method = "ROI")))
}
basis <- tibble::tibble(gamma = c(50, 100, 200)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(excess = purrr::map_dbl(gamma, invested_on, X = Re),
                total  = purrr::map_dbl(gamma, invested_on, X = R),
                ratio  = total / excess)
stopifnot(all(basis$ratio > 1), diff(range(basis$ratio)) < 1e-4)   # one ratio at every gamma
basis
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   gamma excess total ratio
#>   <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1    50 0.387  0.636  1.64
#> 2   100 0.193  0.318  1.64
#> 3   200 0.0967 0.159  1.64
```
:::


At every $\gamma$ the total-return problem invests
64% more of the portfolio in
risky assets than the excess-return problem, because it credits each risky
series with the bill's 2.2% a year as
if that were a reward for bearing risk. The extra holding is not a view about
the assets; it is an arithmetic error about the alternative, and it is why the
data block of every chapter subtracts the bill before anything else is done.

## Key Takeaways {.unnumbered}

- Simple returns add across assets and log returns add across time. The
  arithmetic mean is the input to every objective, the geometric mean is what
  was earned, and the gap is half the variance [@eq-03-drag]. Annualizing a
  Sharpe ratio by $\sqrt{12}$ assumes independence across months, and
  @eq-03-lo says by how much autocorrelation breaks it [@lo2002].
- Returns enter every optimizer in excess of the Treasury bill: the tangency
  portfolio is defined relative to a riskless rate [@tobin1958],
  `PortfolioAnalytics` has no argument for one, an uninvested fraction then
  earns exactly what the objective assumes, and the bill moves. The
  money-market series are not the bill.
- $\mu_{\boldsymbol{w}} - \tfrac{\gamma}{2}\sigma^2_{\boldsymbol{w}}$ is a
  second-order approximation to expected utility [@vonneumann1944;
  @markowitz1959] whose value is a certainty equivalent and whose $\gamma$ is
  a price: at $\gamma = 4$, ten percent of volatility costs
  200 basis points a year [@tbl-03-gamma].
- A portfolio dominates another if it has at least as much expected return and
  at most as much volatility, with one inequality strict; a better allocation
  lies to the northwest, and an asset nothing dominates is efficient. On this
  sample 12 of the sixteen series are dominated
  before any optimizer runs.
- `risk_aversion` in `PortfolioAnalytics` is $\gamma/2$. Under full investment
  a rising $\gamma$ converges to the minimum-variance portfolio, not to cash;
  with the budget relaxed the risky composition is fixed and the invested
  fraction is proportional to $1/\gamma$, which is two-fund separation.
- Strategic allocation is the long-run policy from unconditional moments;
  tactical allocation deviates from it on conditioning information. Chapters
  9 to 15 are strategic, 16 to 19 tactical, 23 to 25 about implementing and
  evaluating either, and the measure a portfolio is judged by must be the one
  it was chosen by.
